utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am ready. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just bear in mind we still have a witness waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe we were on notebook -- the notebook that has been marked for identification purposes as 333. So with the assistance of the court usher, I would like you to look at the notebook. And in particular I would like you to look at what has been marked for identification purposes from that notebook as P258. And I believe you may be able to find it with the last numbers as 632. And for the record it would be P258/D is what I'm asking the gentleman to look at and the English translation of that would be found on P258/C. Have you had a chance to look -- find the page, sir? Perhaps it might be easier to also provide the gentleman with Exhibit P258 so he can make the comparison.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the notebook in front of me and the page with the number. So 00800632.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if that is the page, then I do have that page in front of me that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just for the record, if you could look at the copy that has been marked for identification purposes as P258/D, if you could look at that and tell us whether that is a true, accurate, and fair copy of what appears in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the Bosnian interpretation of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we must have a technical problem. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't hear the Bosnian translation again. I can hear the interpreter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you could be so kind as to try to make a comparison between the copy, which is marked at the bottom of the page as P258/D, with the notebook which has the numbers at the top of the page as 632.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the way this copy looks and the page with this number, it is a copy of the page from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could direct your attention towards the bottom of the page -- pages, in particular to the one message that appears to have been taken at I believe it's 2126. Can you look at that, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that message.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you look at that message, would it not, sir, be true that that message is a summary, as opposed to a verbatim message of what might have been heard and what might have been recorded by your unit when you were supervising it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by a summary, but according to the practice that we had, this is just additional information for the centre which processed this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Maybe we can just revisit some of the issues we talked about yesterday. Please correct me if I'm wrong. As I understand it, the practice was to try to locate a conversation and upon doing so, to record it, tape record it that is, and thereafter to faithfully, diligently, accurately transcribe it word for word, verbatim. Was that not the practice that was put in place in the unit in which you served? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the school, textbook example, of the practice that should have been followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Given this answer, might we conclude that the textbook approach, the textbook practice, which you were taught and, I take it, you were supposed to follow, was that always followed by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with this remark. The primary thing was to carry out the orders of the command. Each order meant that there was certain problems in its implementation that needed to be resolved out in the field. So the primary objective was to carry out the order as fully as it was possible to carry it out regardless of the problems which we may come up against. And there is no need for me to go into those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, first, no one is saying that the practice was right or wrong, but what I am showing you is a deviation of what was supposed to be the practice, the one you which told us when the Prosecutor was questioning you, and that is, that you would tape-record the conversations and have them transcribed verbatim, as opposed to making summaries of conversations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I'm being asked a question here in a way in which this issue cannot be treated. Two experts from the area that we are dealing with, or let's say two soldiers, let's rule out the experts, know exactly how an order needs to be carried out. If someone else who is not in this field looks at this order, it doesn't have the same significance for him as it would for a soldier who is supposed to carry out this order. If this was to be so, then in the world it would be enough to have just one profession for any kind of job. But in this case, in order to interpret an order and carry it out in the actual doing of it, you need people to know how far this order reaches, how possible it is to implement it, and whether it has been carried out fully or whether there were deviations from it. If I did not act according to orders, then my command would have to take disciplinary measures against me, and then that would mean perhaps going to court or some punishment or so on. As far as I know, I have never been reported for any kind of a violation and I was certainly never convicted of any violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we assume, sir, that in carrying out your orders that seemed to have been somewhat liberally interpreted by you, given your position, that sometimes the practice was to try to tape-record an entire conversation and then transcribe it, write it out, faithfully. And then on other occasions to simply jot down a few notes, something that might be interesting, or make a summary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea was to get a faithful conversation. The voracity or the faithfulness of the conversation -- not the faithfulness, but the need to transcribe the conversation from the tape depended on the assessment of how important the conversation was. Unfortunately, it would happen that on the channels people would speak unlinked dialogues. They would mention names which had nothing to do with anything which could not be put in the dialogue. But, for example, if a person noted down these contacts for a long time which were not in the form of a conversation, in a way, they would gather a collection of information which could be interesting for the centre to be able to find out the location of those people. And from the locations from where these people were speaking from, they could identify perhaps the units which would perhaps be active in the zones where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one more exhibit in line of this chapter of my cross. I can go into it or just for the record note that it would be P237, which also demonstrates that it's a mere summary and not an actual verbatim conversation transcribed. I can -- given that we're short of time, I can confront the witness or move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you claim that, I think we better have a look at this piece of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Perhaps we could give the gentleman what has been marked as P237 for identification purposes. And for the record, it would also -- we should also give the gentleman P322, that would be the notebook from which this intercept or partial intercept comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you're now being shown two pieces of document. One would be the notebook and in the notebook if you could be so kind as to flip to the page that is 00778906 at the top right-hand corner. And for the record, that would be found on P327/B. If you could look at that and look at the bottom of the page at the notation, the handwritten notation that was taken at approximately 0834 hours. If you could please first compare the notebook with the copies that were made of the notebook by the Prosecution. Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously a copy of the page of which the last three numbers are 906.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct. Now, if we go to the top of the page, clearly we see a mere notation of what might have been a conversation that was intercepted as opposed to the conversation itself verbatim, the textbook approach that you were taught to apply in the field, particularly given the position that you held there at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that conversation at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But it's not a verbatim conversation, is it? It's merely a notation of a conversation or a summary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my recollection and the information that is given here, this conversation was not particularly relevant for the command. The gentleman who is mentioned in the conversation and whose name is noted down here, or one of the gentlemen that is being mentioned was a commander of one of the brigades of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I didn't even know why somebody would be mentioning that man, and I didn't know whether the command needed to be informed of this. But the intention at the time was, if I remember correctly, to inform the command that there was a demand or a request on the enemy's side to meet with one of the commanders of the BH army. That was quite sufficient. All the other information regarding to the weather, the rain, or whether it was cloudy was not important, and we would be wasting our precious time in transcribing such information. I believe that the information in the form as it is here was in keeping with the guidelines that we had been given by the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is that it's not a verbatim conversation, but merely a summary of -- part of the conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Viada --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is evident from the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm sorry. I have to object because the answer to the question has been very clear in the record. So it's a kind of speculation of extracting too much, perhaps the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Viada. Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Gladly. This is not a verbatim conversation transcribed, but rather, it is a mere -- it is a portion, a summary of a conversation that took place and overheard by your unit. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this conversation here you have participant X and Jevdjevic. The participant X said that Semso Muminovic asked Pandurevic to call him on frequency 144.500. So I believe that -- I mean, it was a long time ago, so I believe that this participant, who I didn't know who it was, informed the other participant that this person from the Bosnian side was requesting this meeting. So we cannot look at this as a summary. We can look at it as one sentence which was transcribed verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's the level of your education, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a university education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move to another intercept. This would be from the notebook that comes under P33 -- P333. And specifically I will be asking you to look at the pages or the page that ends with 618. And for us -- for the rest of us, we could look at P245/G, /G. And I should note that 245/F is the translated version. First, sir, I would like you to look at those two exhibits and to make sure that the copy that is P245/G is the same that appears in the notebook under P333 in the pages that end with 618.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see here means that I have the original and the photocopy of the page which has been marked with the last three numbers 618.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would like to show you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like to show you another exhibit because we're going to do a comparison by what another unit was able to transcribe from the same conversation. So if you would look at what has been marked by the Prosecution as 2 -- as P245/B, the English translation of it would be P245/A. And that would be from notebook 327 -- or P327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Viada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I have to object to this kind of question, because I'm not sure that the witness is in a position to answer this kind of question, cooperation from two different units. He was only working in one unit. And the cooperation with the work of other units is not proper for this kind of witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have not heard the question put forward by the counsel. Let's see what kind of comparison that the counsel is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at what has been marked as P245/B, that would be /B, that would be at the bottom of the page. And it actually goes on to the following page. And at the top of the pages the numbers would be ending with 535.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the document you're referring to, I have two pages in front of me bearing the numbers 535 and 618.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct. Now, if you could look at both of those separately, the one that has -- that ends with 618 was generated from a notebook from your unit, while the other one was generated by another unit in another location. But first, I would like you to just -- to look at both of these intercepts and to tell us whether they would appear to be the same conversation being monitored by two different units in two different locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, to intervene. I just wanted to indicate if it would save time as I advised Mr. Karnavas yesterday, the next witness will be dealing with this -- one of the particular conversations and this particular conversation shortly. Consequently, I don't think it's really necessary to go into it at this point with this witness who actually as I understand it did not intercept either conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, before the gentleman took the stand, out of courtesy and in order to save time, I informed Ms. Issa that the gentleman be provided with both copies, because I would be going into this matter. Secondly, the gentleman was brought in by the Prosecution as holding a particular position, and then there was a line of questioning with respect to his position and with respect to the quality-control process or practice that was put in place. They also elicited certain questions -- or answers from the gentleman with respect to the practice and what would happen when they could not hear certain portions of the conversation. The Prosecution's theory is that these intercepts, by and large, are true, accurate, complete, and reliable, something that is contested both by the Blagojevic Defence team and by the Jokic Defence team. The one that I am showing the gentleman is generated from a notebook which the Prosecution is trying to bring in and authenticate and lay the foundation through this particular witness. Obviously because of his position also he's been able to flip through it, identify it, and I think it's only fair for him to be able to see whether a particular intercept that is included in a notebook from his particular notebook is as it purports to be according to his testimony. I also want to show him another version of an intercept from another location, and what we will see are some stark differences. Things that are missing primarily from the notebook that the gentleman has and also where they've indicated that they could not hear certain portions of a conversation, they would put three dots to note that it was inaudible or they could not understand it. And we will see that in their particular version portions that are missing, assuming that they were said because they are included in the other intercept, we do not have the three dots. What I'm trying to establish here is the unreliability of these particular intercepts, and that's the whole purpose of it. Simply because he didn't author it, and I'm not sure whether he did, because yesterday he did indicate he authored a summary, albeit he was -- in trying to come forward and admit that. Nonetheless, I think he is qualified to comment about the intercept in a notebook from his unit. And assuming that he can read the handwriting in the other notebook, I see no reason why he cannot make the comparison. Assuming he cannot read the handwriting, we took the page -- of giving a copy to the translators so they could read it for him, just in case there might have been a problem with him reading the penmanship. But I think this is classic confrontation, compare and contrast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will hear what the witness is going to tell us. But, Mr. Karnavas, I don't think you can go very far in this aspect, so long as, you know, this witness is not the true author of that particular evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I merely wanted to point out the deficiencies, not the reasons behind them. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity to compare the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I'm facing a very complex task here in a place like this and before the Trial Chamber. What this requires is an analytical approach, you must closely monitor the document portion by portion which again requires a very high level of concentration. This necessarily affects my conclusion. I can't posit my conclusion with precision, because I don't have the sufficient time to be able to establish some sort of accurate comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, how about if I were to present you with a copy that highlighted -- that highlights the distinctions in the two, might that be able to assist you? So why don't I -- I understand you do have it, and also I understand that in the copy you were provided, not only is it highlighted, but you will see some corresponding numbers, "one, one, two, two," and it goes all the way to nine, thereby focusing your attention to the particular portions in each document, the corresponding sections. So in essence, there's not a not a whole lot of analytical process of someone of your calibre and your education and your engineering background would need in looking at these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I have to intervene again, Your Honour. But first of all, that sarcastic comment was totally unnecessary. I don't think I need to say anything more about that. Secondly, we're going to be here a very long time having this witness compare the two documents when we have another witness waiting to testify about this very thing. I mean, We know there are differences in the documents. I don't think there's a mystery in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that you have already made your point and you just want to point out there's some problems in those two documents and you're not going into the very reasons of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct. But the gentleman here has not told us that he sees that there are some gaps. So I need to hear it from -- I'm pointing it for the record and I can't make the record -- well, I can but I can't testify. I'd love to but I can't. That's why if I can hear the gentleman admit and acknowledge that at least there are some areas in his intercept that are not -- that the other intercept does not have, for instance, number 1. And if we were to go down to, say, number 2, number 4, number 6, number 7, number 8, and number 9 that are included in his version are missing -- those are portions that are missing in his version but are included in the other version. Whereas, point number 3 and point number 5 are totally different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you know the Prosecution has agreed that there are some differences in those two documents. And if a particular point is not that crucial to your client, I don't think you have to go through this kind of practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Might I just go through one, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, just point it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could focus your attention on what has been marked as 4, the line number 4, in your document. And if you were to look at the corresponding number 4 that would be found on P245/B, the other document that ends with the numbers 535. You would agree with me, sir, would you not, that what is included in the other document is not included in the document from your unit. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have spent a long time in my civilian life doing certain jobs that require a high degree of accuracy. I find it very difficult to understand if someone is trying to put me in a situation where under stress I should be made to study in only a couple of minutes something that someone else had previously spent months studying and analysing. Anything I say here, any assessment I make, would be superficial and lacking in-depth analysis. In my experience, I can't justify any conclusions and I don't venture into these situations when I do not feel I can answer for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can do it one of two ways. I mean I'm used to spending hours with this sort of a witness. Obviously we are not going to do that here nor do I wish to do that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The other approach is for me to meet with the Prosecutor, if they're willing to concede as I point out to them as their own translator should have pointed out to them, specifically and, then we can enter that into the record as a document. But I think that what my point is that contrary to what the gentleman has testified under oath when he was testifying for the Prosecution, the procedure was far from perfect, was far from accurate, and was far from verbatim and that they didn't even follow their own practice which is when portions were missing or they could not hear portions, there would be dots placed. Again, I want to stress to the Court that punctuation has been a major concern for us given the one particular witness so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, in the cross-examination there is no need for the witness to give an answer which is entirely to your satisfaction because we have the documents. I think that both the Defence counsel and the Prosecution have that document. I think you have already made your point, so there is no need to spend much more time on that issue. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. It's not to my satisfaction. I'm trying to make a record, but I would agree with you and again I want to also stress that with certain witnesses I also want to point out that at some point I will be arguing their lack of credibility. But in light of the answers and in light of the Court's ruling, I have no further questions with respect to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask several questions, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify a number of points concerning your biography before we move on to a number of specific conversations that you entered into this notebook. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, if you would like to ask more questions about the background of this witness, you have to understand that this witness is under the protective measures and we could easily go to private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree, Your Honour. I was going to move to go into private session after my third question. If you believe it's necessary now, we can, no problem with me. But my original plan was to ask the first four questions and then to go into private session, or rather, closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you feel safe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it usual for the corps commander to give out such an order --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please. The interpreters couldn't hear the best part of the question, due to the fact that the microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, would you please repeat your question with the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it normal procedure, is it pursuant to the rules of service that the corps commander should order the transfer of a soldier from one unit to another, or is this usually done by personnel administrators in these units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must remind you, although you probably saw this in my statement, of my position in the unit. I was an ordinary soldier. I was not even a professional soldier. As for organisational issues and the structure of the military, this is something that is usually the job of professional soldiers and not of individuals who merely did their military service, their regular military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I take it, then, that your level of military education would have entitled you to say that you didn't know whether this was within the area of competence of the corps commander or within the area of competence of personnel administrators with those specific units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I'm not familiar with the way orders circulated within the army. I believe that should be the answer to your question, but I can't provide a yes or no answer. In order to do that, I should have to analyse your question which would take up a lot of time, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Practically from 1994 after going through a month of training, you joined the electronic surveillance unit. Am I right in claiming that until July 1995 you had spent about ten months with that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This ten-month period, in your opinion, was that sufficient to qualify you for carrying out those activities and tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does it mean to be qualified to carry out a certain task? Usually it means to meet a number of conditions. I only had a month of training, and my knowledge of equipment was very basic. Usually people are trained for 15 or 20 years to specialise in operating this equipment. We didn't have the time and we did the best we could. We made the best of it, whatever we could learn during the course, and we tried to apply the knowledge acquired during our training. Now, how qualified or professional our work was, I think we need more time to tell. I would have been very happy if I'd had 20 years of military education behind me when I started performing these tasks. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that you had the elementary knowledge to carry out these tasks with the electronic surveillance unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic skills, the professional knowledge, this means that you would have had to be very good at that. I can't say if it was elementary knowledge. Certainly what we knew was sufficient to meet the requirements of the command, the command where individuals worked who had been educated in the former Yugoslav army, and they were knowledgeable enough to assess whether our skills were sufficient or not. Now, you chose to call it elementary. I can't say how elementary it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that in addition to the basic skills you have just spoken about from the area, first of all you need to have good hearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would like to go into private session now for several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please give us a hand with this. There was an exhibit that was shown to you yesterday and we would just like to clarify something about that. If we can have Exhibit P233/F from binder P345 marked for identification purposes as 01077809.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, we have a spare copy for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We discussed this intercept yesterday. If you can please just help me clarify a number of issues in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just please help us and tell us, line 7, what does this mean, the thing behind the letter V, dots, brackets, unclear as if premodulated [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been long since I last looked at this notebook. I no longer work on the same job. I stopped doing this kind of thing as soon as I left the army in April of 1996. This term, "premodulated," I really can't remember any longer what exactly it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, if you look at this, you can see that it was not clear what the other participant in the conversation had been saying. Why wasn't it clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This definition and the use of the term "premodulated" is an attempt to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I therefore conclude that this intercept was not sufficiently clear at the time you recorded it and listened to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was about this line 7, and it states clearly there that in that part we were not able to hear what the speaker said. But if you want to say that applies to the whole conversation, then logically we should then put unclear everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that in the place where there are dots the way you described it in the examination-in-chief, that that is what you did not hear or you were not able to decipher what was being said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be one of two things. In principle, as far as I can recall, these could be also pauses in the conversation or some waiting time. But most often in places where something was unclear, I would try to write it down because markings were sometimes unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can also direct you to the next page, the last paragraph, so for the transcript 01077810. The words three dots, "We are all engaged to the maximum" and then we have, "believe me," then we have three dots, then the text again, and then the word: "Since this morning, we have been reporting." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, that is towards the bottom on the second page with the number 810.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this word "believe me," is pronounced in the Ijekavica dialect, but the word "izvestavanje," "reporting" is in the Ekavica dialect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a language expert, but that's the way it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in the Ekavica dialect, this is used on the right side, on the right bank of the River Drina, so in Serbia. And Ijekavski accent is used on the left bank of the River Drina in Bosnia, in principle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you, not even as an educated person. I would like to remind you that if you look into it that the majority of my professors were Serbs and even I spoke Ekavski dialect for a while and was corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I then reformulate my question, rephrase my question, and say that the majority dialect that is spoken in Serbia is Ekavski and Ijekavski is the majority dialect spoken in Bosnia? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is evident that Ekavski is used in Serbia. Yes, that is evident. But in Bosnia we had both Ekavski and Ijekavski. We had many people coming from Serbia so they used the Ekavski dialect and they used that also in schools. On the other hand, in the time when this notebook was created the official tendency was in Bosnia to speak Ekavski on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So based on this sentence, we can conclude that the speaker in this sentence speaks both Ekavski and Ijekavski. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. If this was faithfully transcribed, it means that that person was mixing Ekavski and Ijekavski.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you said "If this has been faithfully transcribed." If that is so, can I conclude that perhaps you did not, if this is your handwriting, did not faithfully transcribe what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is always the possibility that a man makes various mistakes. Even if the same conversation is transcribed twice, these mistakes can be made. People are not robots. We only have identical copies made by computers now. A person, human being can make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, I agree with that. And in that context I would like to ask you a few more questions, but perhaps this is the appropriate time to make a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we still have five minutes. How long will your questions last? Maybe from your direction, yourself time is up. But from mine, there's still five or seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that I will not need more than 20 minutes more, maybe not even that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Try to finish your cross-examination during this sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I would like to ask the usher, please, to show the witness exhibit -- and for the record it's an intercepted conversation which is in the notebook marked P337, page 00801255 for the transcript. We have prepared excerpts in English from this exhibit which we received from the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you one question. Can you remember whether you identified ever in these intercepts the voice of an officer named Jocic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I do not even remember who Jocic was, nor do I remember his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The intercepts that you have in front of you, I assume that you will agree with me that that is your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you recorded on the third channel participants -- conversations where one of the participants was Jocic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me say it again, at this point you cannot remember that voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the voice, nor do I remember who that man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. You said that you managed to recognise a few voices during the conversations that you listened to in that period, for example, the voice of General Simic, General Tolimir, and General Zivanovic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise those voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Both previous conversations which you recorded and you listened to, you listened to on the third channel on the 14th of July, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you're thinking of these conversations which are marked 255 on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a date there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that it was on channel 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For one conversation it states that it was the third channel, for the second and third it doesn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this conversation we had earlier was, as you said yesterday, in response to the question of the Prosecutor and afterwards looking at it, did take place on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I established -- in order to establish that it was on the 14th of July, I would have to check the beginning of the notebook, and the end, and possibly some other dates, as well as the cycles of the conversations, at what time they began and what time they finished. But this notebook here, this is what I would have to do with this notebook here. I would have to do it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about this past conversation when yesterday you identified that it was a conversation on the 14th of July at 2227 hours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, sir, you have to tell me whether you are talking about this notebook that is in front of me or whether you are asking me about something that happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the previous conversation, not this conversation or this notebook that you have in front of you, but I'm asking you about a previous conversation that you had yesterday in front of you and which you identified had taken place on the 14th of July at 2227.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me what your question is for that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the participant Jocic -- Jokic from Palma and Vilotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a conversation at 2227. I don't have the exact information. I noted yesterday that this did take place on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's correct. I wanted to ask you whether in preparation for your testimony and in conversations with the OTP, did you hear or did they ask you about whether there was a mistake in the name, is it General Vilotic and is it possible that this is actually General Miletic? Did the Prosecutor ask you questions to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're trying to say with your abbreviation OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It refers to questions from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Prosecutor is concerned, this question -- this possibility Miletic or Vilotic was not a question that they put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear before or recognise the voice of General Vilotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time after such a long time ago, I do not remember the man or his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, after such a long time ago, can you remember whether you ever recognised the name of an officer called Jokic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that I recognised the voice of such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that we talked about a little earlier, do you allow for the possibility that the person who introduced himself as Jokic, because of poor audibility or a poor signal, could have been called Djokic or Jocic. Is there such a possibility, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are more theoretical rather than practical possibilities. In principle, it depends. I don't know. As far as I'm concerned, I tried to be as precise as possible, especially when we're talking about the participants. So I avoided putting down anything that was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, when you're listening to the conversation, could you locate the place where General Vilotic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the task of the team that worked with me. The team practically did the job of listening, monitoring, tapping. The task of locating places is an analytical task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this was not your job, are you saying that you don't know where General Vilotic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that he was on channel 3 at that point, as far as I was concerned -- if that was on channel 3, if I recall that conversation well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was on channel 3, so based on that we can conclude that the second participant whom you indicated as Jokic was also on channel 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a conversation between two speakers which was recorded on one channel, it must mean that I recorded the conversation from that channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not concerned and it was not your job to know where they were physically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. Could you tell us whether you know where the seat of the participants from Palma was actually located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Palma was actually the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't know its location. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're thinking about the geographic location, I can't tell you. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From your military training, do you know that a given point in time in a brigade or the brigade command, you would have the duty officer of the barracks, the staff duty officer, and the operations duty officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that your questions are a little bit broader than my knowledge is as a regular soldier. I would like to say that right until the beginning of the war, I was just a regular soldier and that automatically by the end of the war, I was given the rank of non-commissioned officer. But during the war, I was just a regular soldier. And as a regular soldier, I don't know if I would know anything like that. The command did not enable us to learn about the structure of the command and the other elements which were relevant for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude that you don't know that there was a barracks duty officer, a staff duty officer, and an operations duty officer in the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about these terms before. I've heard them before and I've heard them now, but how it functions, where all these things are located, and so on, is not something I actually thought much about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me bring this to a close. Am I right if I conclude that the identification of these two participants, General Vilotic and Jokic, Duty Officer of Palma, arrives from their own personal identification, so that is what you heard and what you noted down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is quite exclusive and gives only one option. In order to establish or identify a person, we can also do that based on the conversation of the exchange operators who are actually establishing the connection. So we don't need to do that purely from the conversation of the participants themselves. Identification, for example, if you recognise the voice of an important person, this important person would never say what their name is and they don't even make calls on such channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that as theory, but I'm asking you specifically now, and please I'm asking you to help me. Regarding this specific conversation and the answers that you have given, that you do not recognise the voices of General Vilotic or Palma Duty Officer Jokic, is this identification based on the fact that they themselves introduced themselves in the course of this intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-120 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that identification can come from the fact that the persons introduced themselves or from voice recognition or from introductions made by those establishing the connection. So I don't know whether they introduced themselves. I don't know that. I don't remember the text of the conversations. I don't have it in front of me. Perhaps the telephone operators said the names. My assumption is that I never -- I do not recall ever recognising the voice of Vilotic. Perhaps this was written in the text itself, so that is how I was able to name the speakers. Sometimes in the course of a conversation, it would often happen that we wouldn't know who was talking unless the people themselves said so or unless the telephone operator establishing the connection in accordance to a procedure would tell his colleague who he's looking for, who is the person looking for that person, why they are looking for that person, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to finish now, Your Honours, but in view of receiving such a general answer from the witness, I would like again for the third time to show the witness Exhibit P233/F and also from notebook 345, I would to show him page 01077809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, is this necessary? I think you have made your point clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honours believe that it is clear enough, then I have no further need to do this. I would just like to show that both participants introduced themselves. The witness here noted that down, and that is the reason or the basis on which he identified the participants. And if this point is clear, then I do not need to show the exhibit to the witness for the third time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have no doubt about that. Everything is clear in that piece of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct, Mr. Viada?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender from both parties? Mr. Viada?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution will be tendering all intercepts and all the notebooks after the last witness. And we will not tender anything at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. How about the piece of paper bearing the witness's name?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: This was a mistake. I'm not sure if we have -- oh, yes. Your Honour, the witness identified himself in the record, even he spelled his own name. Then it's not necessary to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I noticed there are some mistakes on the corrected transcript. We went to private session for that. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. I believe yesterday I showed the gentleman the translations of what was P255/F, and that was marked, the translation, as D75/1. And again, the translation of P255/D, and that was marked as 76/1. There was testimony with respect to this. It wasn't translated by the Prosecution. We do think they're relevant and we would move for their admission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any objections to Mr. Karnavas's proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have an objection. We stand by what we have said, and that is that intercepts should not be admitted until we finish with all of these witnesses. As far as we're concerned, we do not have any documents that we wanted to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That is an objection, if I understand it in the right way. Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry that we could not admit your document into the evidence at this stage. I hope at a later stage you could also submit to us a list of all those intercepts you want to be admitted into the evidence, and then we'll consider it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. During the break, the usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home. Thank you very much. And we'll have our break and we'll resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon, Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And, sir, you are a protected witness, so we will start by showing you a piece of paper and ask you to confirm whether or not that is your name by just indicating yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If I can just have the assistance of Madam Usher, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, that is Exhibit P352.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Just to start with your background, sir, I understand that you are from Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that you -- your religious faith is Muslim. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges briefly about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I can. I completed my elementary and secondary education in my native town. I studied technical sciences for a while, but I interrupted my studies because money was quite short at the time. There were many of us in the family, so there was no money for me to complete my studies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And at some point, sir, in your life did you develop an interest in radios and did you participate in amateur radio activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: When did you develop your interest in radios?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I was quite young at the time. I may have been 17 or 18 years of age. That's when I first became familiar with the equipment and the way it was used. I realised what it was, that it was a very good thing, a very useful thing, that you could talk to someone long distance without even knowing the person by using special signs speaking to the person in our language or in English. I really liked it and I became an enthusiast.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And in developing your interest in radio, sir, did you pursue a certificate or some sort of education in pursuit of that interest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. I took an exam to obtain a category C for ham radio operators. And then I had to keep on training myself. And then I took an exam to obtain the B category license. And that's the most advanced license that I have for ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, receive that license or certificate, the B category?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. I obtained the certificate for B category.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Now, dealing with your service in the army, did you serve with the JNA at some point, and if so, what years did you perform that service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, I did compulsory military service with the former JNA in 1981 and 1982.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And if you -- did you specialise in your military service during that period of time, and if so, what specialty did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the signals branch. So while I was in the army, I also took an exam for the military B certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And during that period of time, sir, did you become familiar with JNA radio equipment that was available in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Turning then your attention, sir, to the war in Bosnia that started in 1992, I understand that you became part of the electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic warfare unit as part of the Bosnian Muslim military forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And in that capacity, sir, generally speaking, what were your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: My basic duty was to intercept communications, the communications of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you served, in fact, in this type of unit until the end of the war. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And from the period of 1992 until the end of the war, whose enemy communications were you intercepting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: The communications of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And just very briefly, sir, can you tell us what were the locations in Bosnia where you worked in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in 1992 until the end of that year, for the first couple of months we were on a hill near our town. And then we were transferred to an elevation called Okresanica. In 1994, I was again transferred to a different location where short wave emissions by the Army of Republika Srpska were being intercepted. As of spring 1994, I was transferred to Konjuh. I stayed there until December when the war was over. I stayed there until the very end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And while you were at Konjuh, sir, in what capacity did you serve at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I worked there as an operator. I operated the equipment, the tapping equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Other witnesses have testified about the procedures that you used when you were at Konjuh, sir. So I'm not going to ask you very detailed questions in relation to that, but I will ask you if you can just very briefly explain the process or what you did when you intercepted a conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: There was an established procedure. In the room we had several devices, several pieces of equipment, sometimes four, sometimes five, sometimes a piece of equipment would break down and then need fixing. All those were receivers, just receivers. We would receive signals from telephone frequencies from the radio relay 800 and radio relay 1. These devices were always on. Those were so-called scanners. These devices were used to scan various frequencies. Sometimes they would stop -- they would stop whenever a signal appeared on a given frequency. We would stop the machine right there. We would start the reel-to-reel recorder that was linked to the other piece of equipment. We would record the conversation and stop the recorder afterwards. Or we would press the pause button. After that, we would decide if the conversation was urgent or important, if the conversation was about offensive operations or about private matters, something of no relevance to us. It was left to our discretion to decide on the relevance of a given conversation. If the conversation was important, we would immediately rewind the tape and transcribe the conversation into a notebook that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And once you transcribed the conversation into the notebook, what would happen next? What would you do with the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: If we deemed the information contained in the conversation important or if names were being dropped that we thought were important, we would call another person to come over, a person who was helping us with computers. The received text would then be typed into a computer. The person operating the computer would then code, encrypt, this information and forward it to our centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the process of getting the signal and pressing the button on the tape recorder to tape the conversation, is it possible that a small amount of information was not recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the leading nature of the question. The question can be rephrased. But the Prosecutor -- I know we're trying to rush it, but she should be in a habit of asking non-leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa, you may put your question is a neutral way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I thought this was the part where we weren't really going to spend too much time on it. But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know, during the previous witnesses I think this issue is a heated debate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: When you tape-recorded a conversation, sir, did you always manage to capture the entire conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Not always, no. Sometimes we did succeed and sometimes we just couldn't. The scanner must scan a number of frequencies before it encounters a signal. So sometimes it was possible to miss out on a portion of the conversation before the scanner stopped. This was possible. It was the case sometimes that we failed to record something that was already being said on a given frequency.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, the information, sir, that was not captured on tape, was that somehow captured in another form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: This information, if there was something that we heard and yet failed to switch on the tape recorder, if this was something important, names of participants or anything like that, code names perhaps, we would write them down immediately at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Is there anywhere else where you may note down information of this nature, other than the notebook, at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. At the outset we didn't even have notebooks, so we used sheets of paper. Later on we had notebooks and the order was for us to write this down into those notebooks. So later, we only used notebooks and then the whole thing would, of course, then be transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if there was a doubt about what was said on the communication when you were listening to the tape at the time, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: When listening, if there was something that we weren't sure about, we would put a question mark. If we couldn't hear something at all, a whole portion, we would just put dots. If by listening to the tape, it wasn't possible to ascertain what was said. So we were using an established system of signs, a question mark if there was something we weren't sure about. If something was just missing, we would put dots there and that's how we would copy the whole thing into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Would you write anything down that you weren't sure about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: While taking the conversation down, we wrote down exactly as we heard. And if someone was using this information later on and the person using our transcription couldn't understand what was going on, he would just give us a call to explain. Sometimes we would listen in to a number of conversations at the same time and we would just transcribe what seemed important. So the tape was listened to again, and there was another person who transcribed the conversation. He would come back to us with questions if there was something that was still not clear and then we would instruct him what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when you mean -- when you say we would instruct him what to do, can you explain to us what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: If, for example, he couldn't read someone's handwriting because we did this in a hurry, he would come back to us and say, "What's this word?" and then we would tell him. If, for example, someone noticed an error in the text, he would come back to us and say, "What's this? This must be an error. Can you listen to the tape again, please," and then we would go back to the tape, listen to it again, and give him the final version, the one that he then typed into the computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us how many times you would listen to the tape. You don't have to give us a specific, exact number, but approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which particular tape are we speaking of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's a general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We just want a general answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: If our conclusion was that the information on the tape was crucial, if there was a name being referred to, the time an operation would start, if there was a place being mentioned where manpower or weapons would be sent, those tapes would be listened to over and over again. If something was still unclear, we would just rewind and listen again. If everything was clear, we would just take it down and later transcribe the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we get to a particular conversation, can you just tell us generally, sir, what did you do with the tapes after transcribing a particular conversation? What happened to the tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: You take down the conversation and if there was still room on the tape, you would press the pause button and the next time the scanner stopped catching another frequency, the tape would then be recorded to the end. If there were no spare tapes, midway through a shift, for example, we ran out of tapes and there was no one to give us more tapes, we would use the other side of the tape. And once we've used that up, we would rewind the tape back to the beginning. There was a shortage of tapes at the time. We sometimes even re-used old tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I want to now focus your attention, sir, to a particular conversation. I will be referring to a notebook marked as P327.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for ease of reference, Your Honours, that conversation is binder number 2 under the date of 15 July. I will also be referring to the package which is marked as Exhibit 245.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask you to please turn to the page 00804535.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: A photocopy of that page, Your Honours, is at Exhibit 245/B.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've seen this original notebook in my office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you recognise the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And where does the notebook come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: This notebook was at Konjuh where we received the conversations that we were intercepting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting at page 535 through 537?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is this a conversation that you intercepted, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you transcribed the conversation into this particular notebook. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the very top of the exhibit, two people appear to be identified in this conversation, sir. Who are they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Colonel Ljubo Beara and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And how did you determine that they were the participants in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we would always recognise Krstic's voice, because he spoke on a number of different occasions. You soon became familiar with his voice because he had a very powerful, resonant voice. We always recognised Krstic. If sometimes we didn't catch the introductory part of the conversation where they would introduce themselves, they would sooner or later in the course of the conversation say their names. If there was no way for us to know who the speakers were, we would just put two question marks, speaker A, question mark, speaker B, question mark. But if you look at the text of the message, the way they speak to one another, they kept using their names. So it was easy for us to understand who the participants were. This was the channel, or rather, the frequency that he very often spoke on. It was his phone. There was several ways for us to ascertain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say, "This was the frequency that he spoke on," just to be clear for the record, you're referring to General Krstic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. We had memorised his frequency on our equipment. We often listened to him. It was important for us at the time. He was a very important figure in the Army of Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what frequency that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That's 205.850 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, before we start referring specifically to the conversation or the contents of the conversation, I'd like you to tell the Judges whether you're able to date this particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I'm not able to date this conversation, because I didn't write it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: When you say you didn't write it down, you're referring to writing down the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Precisely, I didn't write down the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Did you -- when you reviewed this notebook in my office, sir, did you -- were you able to provide an approximate date based on other dates in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Well, yes. If I look at the dates before and after, I could say that it was either the 14th or the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And just so that we're clear for the record, sir, I'd like you to turn to page 00804528. And can you tell the Judges what date you see on that page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: On this page, I see 0907, the year is 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So that's 11 July, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. You're quite right. Yes, that's underneath. The 11th of July. This one was at the top of the page, and below you can see the true date this conversation took place. And you're quite right. It's the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd ask you, sir, then to turn to page 537, the last digits 537, and tell us if you see a date on that page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: The 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Now, looking at the conversation itself, sir, the contents of the conversation, is there anything in the conversation that assists you in determining that this conversation took place, either on the 14th or 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, there's this one sentence which Beara said, and that is: "They will not come. There is no other solution but those 15 or 33 with Indjic. Those who were supposed to come on the 13th and did not." So that is that date. And then the next instructions here, what we can see, it means that this conversation was transcribed after the 13th. So it can be either on the 14th or the 15th. So it was before the 16th. This is what I concluded based on what we have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honour, in the translated copy at P245/A, that date in the content of the conversation is found at from eight lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, I'm sorry to interrupt, could you ask the witness what is the frequency that General Krstic was on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I did ask him that, Your Honour, but I will re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some problem in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us, what was the frequency that General Krstic spoke on that you indicated earlier you were aware of he normally spoke on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. The frequency was 255.850.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, turning to Prosecution Exhibit 245/E, which I'm going to ask be placed on the ELMO, please. Just very briefly, can you tell us, sir, what is this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: This document could be a typed report of the conversation which was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: So it's a conversation that was copied into this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And if you can look at the top or the heading of this document, can you please indicate which place is indicated, the location of where the document was generated, as well as the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, it's written down here, Konjuh, the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
