utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, sir, have you reviewed this document when you were in my office along with the conversation that you transcribed in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is the substance of the document, the computer printout, the same as the one in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. The content is the same, except there are some words in one which are not in the other. But the sense of the conversation is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And before we get to those words, sir, can you tell us if you typed the document, the computer version? Did you type that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: No. It wasn't me. It was a young man who was responsible for those things. We typed those things out when we weren't busy and when he wasn't there, but it was usually his job to do the typing and the -- and to enter it into the log.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. I'm now going to ask you some specific questions about the content of the notebook and the computer printout.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for ease of reference, because I don't think we can place both documents on the easel, I'm going to be referring to the translation of the notebook which is found at 245/A and the translation of the typed version which is found at 245/C.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, dealing with some of the differences, sir, in the notebook, can you please look at the top of page 535 in the notebook. And I'm referring you specifically to the words: "Tasic or Sladojevic." Do you see that there, which is four lines from the top in the translated version.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And if you look at the computer printout, the typewritten version, sir, four lines from the top?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Again in the translated version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It says Nastic, the name's Nastic or Blagojevic. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Are you able to explain or account for that particular difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: When I was transcribing the conversation from the tape, at that point that is how I heard it probably. I wrote down the way I heard it. But I was even making some correction here, Sladojevic, but I continued with the transcription not paying attention to the above written names. I thought those were the names. Then as we continue, I see that Blagojevic and Nastic appear. So I wrote down as I received it, as I heard it at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So you're indicating that in your notebook, sir, you later on wrote the proper names of Nastic and Blagojevic. Can you just read out that sentence for us so that we know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: K: I'll see what I can do, but I'll disturb a lot. Please, you have down there at Nastic's and Blagojevic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And later we also see that you referred to the name of Blagojevic two lines down from that: "Check with Blagojevic, take his Red Berets again." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The sentence says: "Check with Blagojevic. Take his Red Berets."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to direct your attention specifically to one other difference, sir. If you can look at the very last line in your notebook at page 0804537.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Where it says: K: I'll see what I can do. Can you indicate, sir, whether there's a difference between that line and the last line of the typed version.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: There is a difference, because in the typed version two words were added which are not there in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what are those two words, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I apologise to everybody, but the words are, "Fuck it."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And the rest of the sentence: "I'll see what I can do," remains the same. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. The rest of the sentence is the same: "I'll see what I can do." But here it says: "I'll see what I can." But the sense of it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. In general terms, sir, when you compared these two documents, are there any other differences that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to the term "general." If the gentleman wishes -- or if the lady wants to point to specific differences because there are some more specific differences, then she should do so. If she wants to rephrase it to say is the conversation in essence the same type versus the handwritten, that's a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We also could not understand what is in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I previously asked him if the conversation was in essence the same and he indicated that it was. I don't plan on going through the particular specifics of it because I don't particularly think it's that important. If Mr. Karnavas wants to go through the specifics of it, he can do so in cross-examination. But I will rephrase my question to perhaps make it a little bit clearer with Your Honour's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just ask if there's any other differences.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, are there any other differences that you notice between the notebook and the typewritten version without having to go through every single one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. I immediately find a difference in this line where Beara says: "Okay. Let's see. They can come to Drago." And then in the typed text it says: "See if they can come to Drago." So there are these differences. But still I see that the sense of the sentence is the same. Two lines above that it says: "I'll see what I can do." But in the typed text it says: "I'll see what I can." So there are also some things that were missed -- well, some words were missed, but the sense of the -- the gist of the sentence remains the same. So I don't really see that much difference there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say the word "do" was missed, you're referring to the notebook or the typewritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That word is missing in the typed text, but the word "do" exists in the text that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you actually compared the two documents very carefully when you were sitting in my office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you note -- did you find that in making these comparisons that the meaning was changed between the typewritten version and the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: No. The meaning stayed the same. The sense of the sentence remains the same. It's just that these words are missing which were not so important for us, and they speeded up the work if we just left them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And did you notice anything in particular about the manner in which the person who typed the conversation wrote?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: The way that it was typed or the way it was written, everybody had their own way of doing it. It was quite rushed, so when he was typing it out if something was unclear to him, he would call us, or if the meaning of a sentence would not be clear to him, he would call us. So that was the way. I don't know what you mean in particular, but I'm just going by what I see here in the notebook in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. In respect of the words that we specifically dealt with, sir, the first example that we dealt with the difference between Tasic and Sladojevic which you later corrected in your notebook and the two words in the bottom at the very end of the conversation, the expletives before, "I'll see what I can do," can you account for these differences? Can you suggest any possibilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, it calls for speculation. The gentleman is now being asked to read the mind of the typist. And unless the gentleman can establish that he had a conversation with the typist, he recollects having this conversation, and now he can articulate the reasons, then I think it's improper. He did give an explanation as to the Tasic and Sladojevic in the first line. I think that was a reasonable inference that can be derived. As for the last, I think it would be improper. It would be asking him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, frankly speaking, we could not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could rephrase it, taking into consideration the objections from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, can you account for these differences based on your knowledge of the procedures that you were working with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. At that point, that's what I heard and that's what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I wrote down as I heard it, first names, last names, and other things. However, when the text was being typed out and sent, then it was important. So the person who was typing it out, if he noticed this difference, he would call all of us or he would just call me who actually worked on it, then we would listen to it again. Then he would ask for the correct information that he should type in. That's what we would tell him. This would be it. What was written before was not correct and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, did the typist normally have the right to add a word or add something that was not normally in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: He did not have that right. It was his duty to type. He didn't listen to it really that much and he didn't have too much time to work on the listening devices. He didn't have time for that. His duty was to type out what we recorded. And he would do it the way we would tell him. It wasn't his job to change anything without our approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Are you normally present, sir, when the typist is typing up the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would object to that, too, Your Honour. Normally -- what is normal. Is it his report or other reports? I don't mean to slow down the process, but this is a rather vague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have no problem, you know, with this question. Normally is normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if the Trial Bench has no problem, then I have no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. You may proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question because this last conversation is still in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Are you normally present when the typist is typing up the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: If the person who is typing it out had something that was not clear to him, then he would call us. But he typed by himself only the things that were clear for him, and there was no ambiguity. He would call us if something was not clear. We were there. It was one big room and we were all working there. Perhaps somebody if they were asleep or something, were not in the room, but otherwise we would all be there, so it was easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain why the -- a word after re-listening to the tape may be added in the typewritten version but not in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: It could be added if this was not clear to the person who was typing. So then he would talk to us and then we would tell him orally to do it. That's what would usually happen, or if we listened to something again, then we would tell him, add this and this. So it would happen only in these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But my question is: Is it only added in the typewritten version and not added as well in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, this one word was. I've found it here. It's not in the notebook and it's in the printed version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm trying to get at, sir, and perhaps I'm just not phrasing my question very well, is: That word that we were looking at or the last two words, the expletive you told us about before, "I'll see what I can do," is in the typewritten version. And you've just now explained to us that if there was a question, you would re-listen to the tape --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to coaching the witness as to what he should say. She can pose the question. Because so far there has been no foundation that this gentleman recalls having gone over with the typist on this particular intercept, having played and replayed the tape, and thus you have those two words, the expletive and the typed version versus the one in the handwritten version. Generically he's told us. Now we're talking about one specific intercept. So unless a foundation can be laid, Your Honour, I think it would be highly improper for the Prosecution to be suggesting the answers and to be coaching the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, the witness answered this question. I found it here. It is not in the notebook and it is in the printed version. So the only question you could ask is one word: Why?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have to give so many explanations so as to confuse everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. I take Your Honour's point. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, sir, why --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why, with a question mark --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a question mark, just why with a little inflection at the end. No further editorialising or coaching, that's all I'm saying the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand you. I quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: But I am not editorialising nor am I coaching. We've just had some discussion about this. I just want to go back and refresh the witness's memory, which I'm entitled to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may repeat the witness's answer and then ask why.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If that's how you want me to do it, I'll do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that those words are in the typed version and not in the notebook. Can you tell us why.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I can't tell you why, really. Because in the written version this word was not important to me, because it doesn't change the sense of the sentence. It's been added here. Perhaps if it was on the tape and the person who was typing it said: Should I add that or not? And I probably told him, yes, add it. He probably heard the word and asked me: Should I add it? And I was able to tell him to do that. Whereas, when I was writing it out in the notebook, this word wasn't so important to me -- it didn't add or take too much away from the meaning, so I didn't put it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just looking at a couple of other things in the content of the conversation, sir, I see there's a reference to the word "Krle," K-r-l-e, and we can see that at the second-to-last sentence in the translated copy. Is that a nickname in your country, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, it's a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And which name does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, this Krle here refers to General Krstic's nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you indicated earlier that it was important to write down the words that you heard and send it to the command. Can you tell us why.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: The words that we heard but didn't manage to record, if they were names, if they were places, we would write them down. So we didn't manage to record them, but we would write them down. So what was recorded we would transcribe later, but if we didn't manage to record everything, we would write down those quickly -- those words very quickly while our minds were still fresh, if this was important. If it was not important, then we wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, was there anything that you may not necessarily write down when you're transcribing a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Vague. Vague, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Ms. Issa, we don't know what's your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I deal with that, Your Honour, in the next segment. It may become clearer rather than asking it at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you the same conversation that was intercepted at another location at Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, I'm going to refer to Exhibit 245/F as being the translated copy and 245/G. And I would ask that the 245/F be placed on the ELMO and 245/G be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you see that conversation in front of you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to look at this conversation in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you first of all tell us how many speakers are captured in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now she's asking the individual to decipher another intercept. Now, in light of the objections that she and her colleague raised with the previous witness, I think unless there's some foundation laid I would have -- I would raise the same objections that they were raising during my presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, first of all I think you have to point out what's the relationship between the 245/A, /C, and this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I thought I did that, Your Honour. It's the same conversation intercepted at Okresanica, the same conversation that was intercepted by the witness at Konjuh. And that is the difference between the category of the previous witness versus this witness. This witness did actually intercept one of the conversations, so he would be in a position to look at the same conversation intercepted elsewhere and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But first you have to ask this witness some questions about this intercept. Whether they are the same intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that they are quite different, but I need your guidance in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated you had an opportunity to review this intercept in my office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And after having reviewed the intercept in my office, is it the same conversation that you intercepted in Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: It is. If you look at the time, I have 10.00, he has 3 minutes to 10.00, so probably he switched on his device 3 minutes before I did. Colonel Beara, he can't hear it -- you only have Colonel Beara speaking here and his speech is transcribed; where, as on the document itself he can see what it says. We can't hear General Krstic. You can only see Colonel Beara speaking; whereas, Krstic can't be heard. Whereas, it's the same conversation. If I look at what specifically Beara said and then compare it, it's the same meaning, the same sentences, which would lead me to conclude that it's the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, based on your experience both at Okresanica and Konjuh, do you have an explanation as to why you were better able to hear the conversation at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. Unless they can identify at this particular time and place. Even though he was able to work at both locations, now we're talking about a specific period. There needs to be a foundation whether during that period the individual was aware of both localities, the receiving aspects, and capabilities of both localities on that particular day. I think that would be the first foundational step that I would require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Issa, lead your witness step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I didn't think that was going to be an issue. As I understood my friend was going to refer to this particular conversation, but I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, when you were at Okresanica, you indicated -- well, let me start here. You indicated you left Okresanica in 1994. Is that correct, in the spring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And when you were at Okresanica, sir, can you explain to us what you were doing there in relation to -- or just tell us very briefly what you were doing there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: The same job as at Konjuh. We had similar equipment or even the same equipment. It's just that Okresanica is not as high an elevation as Konjuh and it was demonstrated that certain phone lines of Republika Srpska could not be caught at Okresanica. There was a lot of interference and it couldn't catch certain frequencies. So we were on the lookout for a higher elevation to try to work with this higher elevation, and that's how the squad at Konjuh was set up. It turned out that we were successful and that the range of the conversations and frequencies received from Konjuh was much wider.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And given that explanation, sir, that you just gave us, with respect to the difference in frequencies and the elevation, looking at the conversation that you -- we just looked at where only Beara is caught -- is captured in the conversation, are you able to explain why it was better heard at Konjuh versus Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. If there's no foundation here, there's no testimony that one place heard this better than the other. This is testimony by the Prosecution. We should swear her in and then I can cross-examine her as well. This is totally improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the witness has answered this question in a certain way. If you look at the transcript, you know, the witness said clear the different positions of the two places. But on the other hand, Ms. Issa, you really are giving the testimony. You should ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, certainly, Your Honour, but I did think the witness indicated that he was familiar with the equipment. He said it was the same equipment. He said that it was a different elevation. He indicated that they had a similar practice. I think with all of that that is sufficient to lay the foundation. I could go on and ask more questions, but we'll be here for quite some time if I have to, you know, ask that many questions to lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there is no objections, I'll let you go, but it seems there is quite an issue for the Defence. So I believe that you need some patience.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I do have patience, Your Honour, I have lots of patience, perhaps more than Mr. Karnavas. I will ask a few more questions. And hopefully that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated earlier that you had similar equipment and similar practice in Okresanica to Konjuh. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were at Okresanica and then subsequently moved to Konjuh, did you notice anything about the frequencies between the two locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Well, we all noticed the difference. At Konjuh, the sound, the received signal was much clearer. All signals -- all the frequencies. We had all been ham radio operators for a long time, and we knew that the altitude was very important for receiving this kind of signal, this kind of frequency. The higher you are, the clearer the signal is. The lower your position is, the less clear the signal. So this was the essential difference between the two locations. That's why Konjuh was better than Okresanica. And the direction the antenna was pointed, that was also important. It has to be pointed in the direction of whoever you're listening in to. There's another difference in the clarity of signal which has to do with the phones and the antenna of the people taking part in the conversation. So those must also be facing each in order for you to see which location is clearer. So whichever location is clearer is likely to receive -- is nearer is likely to receive a much clearer signal. That's another very important difference that affects the clarity of signal and reception. It also depends on the antenna. Sometimes some -- certain kinds of antenna work better at a higher altitude and some don't. This depends on the make of your antenna. Then also there's the weather. Sometimes it there's a storm, it's more difficult to hear and the weather is much clearer in a different location where the reception is much better. So this also determines the difference in the quality of signal and reception in the various locations. When I look at this document which is from Okresanica where one participant is heard, this often happened that we heard the one and not the other. This was nothing unusual. Sometimes there were two participants and for one of the many reasons you couldn't hear the other participant. This was quite often the case and it was nothing new to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I think that is the end of that, Your Honour. Now, I know, Your Honour, we have about five minutes before the break and I'm going to be asking a few more questions in relation to this particular conversation. I don't know if Your Honour wishes to take the break now or five more minutes. I'm in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll continue until you're finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe I'll be finished my entire examination before the break in five minutes. I'm just talking about this particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So how long do you need to finish your entire examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps around 20 minutes, maybe a little bit shorter, Your Honour. I think I'm being liberal in my estimate depending on whether there are objections or not, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, then we'll have a break, a short break. Shall we resume at quarter to 6.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Just looking lack at the conversation, the one we were just dealing with from Okresanica versus the one you took, there's -- I -- we can see there that there's an introduction, an introduction of the parties, and a portion of the conversation at the beginning which you don't have in your notebook. Do you have an explanation for why you don't have that in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I can't remember the specific reason. I can only give you my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, based on your experience, sir, can you give us a possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite possible, because I see that his time is three minutes earlier. So he started listening to the conversation before my scanner caught the frequency. That's one of the possibilities. So he recorded something that I didn't. The second possibility is we both recorded the same thing, except I failed to write down the beginning of the conversation. Can I speak to him? Thank you. Hello. Hello. That's another possibility. I told you before, we used a lot of abbreviations, and it was too many things at a time for me to take down, but they perhaps did. So that's another possibility for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just dealing with one more matter in relation to this conversation, sir, if you look at the conversation, there are references such as "who, what," in the conversation. And by way of an example for Your Honours' reference, it's about five or six lines from the bottom of the translation which is at 245/F. We see a "what, who." That is indicated that Colonel Beara spoke. Do you see that there? I would be referring to P245/G in the B/C/S version. Do you see that there, sir, in the notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you include references to who or what or words of that nature in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I tried to avoid this as often as I could, because this told me nothing and it just took up space in the notebook. It took up tape on the tape, if you like, and it took up a lot of time. So there were often things that I didn't write down. If I had enough time, sometimes I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just referring, then, to Prosecution Exhibit 245/J. I don't know if Madam Usher has that, 245/J. J, yes. If we can just put that on the ELMO very briefly, please. If we can actually put down the second page as well. Okay. Why don't we -- actually, if I can ask Madam Usher to remove the first page very briefly, please -- sorry to remove the top page very briefly and return the first page on to the ELMO. Now, just to save time, sir, you had an opportunity to review this document in my office and compare it to the notes of the Okresanica notebook. Is that correct? It's the one that's sitting on the ELMO, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And you looked at the second page and the heading of the document. Is that correct? I'm sorry, I don't know if that was audible what you said. Could you repeat what you just said, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And the -- can you just briefly tell us the location of this conversation from the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: This was taken down at Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And it's dated July 15, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. The 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And specifically, sir, you had an opportunity to review the conversation on the second page of that document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you compared it to the notes or the -- the notes of this conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And was it the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: It was the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that's how we know it came from Okresanica, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, see there's testimony there. Now, this is improper. And if we were in an Anglo-Saxon court, she could be sanctioned for that. I understand we're not there, but she comes from that tradition and perhaps that's the way they practice where she comes from. But this is highly improper to be suggesting and testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't testifying nor was I suggesting. I was simply indicating something for the record. There is no jury here. I think Your Honours are perfectly capable of making decisions based on the evidence that you hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that's why I believe that your remarks are not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I -- Your Honours, I was simply trying -- I wasn't trying to make a remark in any way to offend the Court. I was simply trying to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no. We could arrive at the same conclusions from the testimony of this witness by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: A point well taken, Your Honour. But I don't really want to comment about Mr. Karnavas's behaviour in the courtroom. Perhaps we can just move on to the next conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, very briefly I'd like to show you a copy of another conversation that is marked --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Just very briefly, I'm referring to 245/K, the English translation, and 245/L, which is a notebook. And this is yet another location. Now, sir, can you -- you've had an opportunity to look at this conversation or this intercept in my office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And after having reviewed it and compared with the conversation that you took down at Konjuh, is it substantially the same as the one you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I won't be asking any specific questions in relation to this conversation. Moving then on to the last conversation I'd like to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I'll be referring Your Honours to the second binder under the August 2nd date, to Exhibit P304. And I also would like to refer to notebook which is at Exhibit Number 341.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you take a look at that notebook, please, that's in front of you and turn to page 00804430 to 431. Is this your handwriting -- do you recognise the handwriting, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you intercept this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the frequency number is in relation to this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: In this conversation, sir, it appears that the participants you have noted down as Krstic and Obrenovic. Can you tell us how you found out that those are the participants or how did you determine that those are the participants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: They introduced themselves, and you can see from the text that they introduced themselves and called each other by name. And then also it was not difficult to recognise Krstic's voice. We didn't have any problem with doing that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Turning then to Prosecution Exhibit 304/D. And the translation that accompanies it which is 304/C. If we can just briefly place the translation on the ELMO and the document, the original, 304/D, before the witness, please. Can you identify this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: This typed document contains the same conversation as the one that I took down here. It's the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just indicate the date for the record, please, and the location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. I noted down the time and the day. I didn't note the date here in my book.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But the date and the -- is there a date in the typewritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. There is a date in the typewritten version, and it's the 2nd of August, 1995, Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you indicate what does the date signify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: This date was entered by our encryption officer while he was typing it, so that means he typed it that day, encrypted it, and sent it on to our centre. So based on that, I would conclude that that's the day the conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Do you draw the same conclusions or different conclusions with respect to the previous conversation we were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you just explain that briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I can. The conversation which is transcribed at a certain time and a certain date into the book, if it's important and if important information appear which we considered to be important, when we finish we type it out, encrypt it, and send it out. There would be a date put in that report, and that's how we would know. I didn't put it down in my book, because I had the habit of thinking that perhaps somebody had already put in the date for that day before me. So I didn't always have to do it, but I think that it was a Wednesday on that day. I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Just a few final questions by way of clarification. Can you explain your practice when intercepting conversations about using the pause button. You mentioned using the pause button before. Can you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Since the tape recorders and the equipment were turned on all the time, the pause button on the tape recorder was always active, so it was always on pause. Nothing was recorded until the conversation was found by the scanner, then we would depress the pause button and the tape recorder would begin to record until the end of the conversation. Later we would activate the pause button again. We would rewind the tape up to a certain counter number on the tape recorder, this is how we would tell how far to rewind. Then we would transcribe the recorded conversation, send it on. It would be typed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And why would you use the pause button in this manner, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: First of all, we were able to activate the recording device much slower. It would take much longer for us to press two or three buttons, then it would take a little bit to get the equipment fully working. So in those few moments, we would perhaps miss on some important information. So it was in order to speed things up. Sometimes there would be another conversation appearing at the same time. We would just depress the pause button and then we would move to this other conversation to begin to record that conversation. So that was the reason we did it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You are exactly within the time limit you promised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for clarification. Perhaps we can get out of here quickly. As I understand it, part of your function was to listen, lock in to a particular conversation, and then faithfully record it, and then transcribe it thereafter. That was part of the process that you specifically were involved in. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you as the operator, because of that pause button, would be able to discriminate between what was nonessential conversation and what was relevant conversation. And so you would use the pause button to occasionally not record, listen in but not record uninteresting conversations and then take the pause button off and only record what was relevant, in your opinion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: We would do that sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it that once you locked into a conversation that you deemed important, you would listen to it and make sure that it was tape recorded properly before you would then go off to transcribe -- write it out into the notebook. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I don't understand. The tape recorder records the way it does. I don't understand what you mean, recorded properly or not. I don't know what you mean by that. It records when you press and then it begins to record, and then it finishes when you stop recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. After you stop recording, was it not part of your function to then rewind and then write out into the notebook what you had heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: If the conversation was not important but it was recorded, we didn't even put it down in the book. But if in our opinion we felt it was important for us because of some data, then we would play back the tape. We would listen to it and note it down in the notebook, according to the procedure that I described before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, would you do that immediately or would you search for another conversation and then perhaps after the tape was at a certain limit, would you then go back and try to transcribe the various conversations that you had recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: It all depended on our priorities, on the priority of the telegram. If it was important for us, we would transcribe it right away, because we wanted to send it on to our centre immediately. But if it wasn't so important in our opinion, we could also pass it along throughout the day, perhaps a couple of hours later or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it some -- as I understand your testimony, somebody else would have to do the typing and the encrypting before it went -- it was sent off. You were not the one doing that if you were the one operating the recording system?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: There was an encryption officer who would encrypt it and send it out. Sometimes we would type also if he didn't have time or if he went somewhere or if something wasn't clear to him while he was typing, he would call us to help him, how he should put something down, what he should put down, if he couldn't read something or if he found a mistake or something, then we would tell him what it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was he located in the same room or was he in a separate room where you were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: He was in the same room. He had his own work station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was it necessary for you to hand over your notebook for him to type out what you had written out based on what you had heard from the tapes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand whether it was a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You may need to repeat your answer to that because they didn't get your answer to that, the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I take it, as you've indicated, there were times when he would not be able to -- he would need your assistance in order to type out what was in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. We wrote fast generally, so our handwriting was perhaps in places not so nice. So he often needed our help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So in general, if I could use that term, when he would need your help is because he's trying to read someone's handwriting and not trying to interpret what was on the recording device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: What wasn't clear to him, he would ask us. He asked us about everything that was unclear to him while he was typing, what was legible, what was clear to him. If he didn't find any mistakes or discrepancies, he would be the one to type it out and send it out by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, am I to understand, and help me out here, that on occasions he would also ask you to play back the tape for him to listen, or was it -- were his questions merely directed to what was written down on the paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: He would tell us to listen to it again. He didn't really interfere much in that. He would be typing out something and then he would say, I didn't quite understand what you wrote here. Perhaps you could help me. So if he didn't understand something, then he would ask us, sometimes several of us, to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was it the practice to go back and re-listen to the tape, even after you had listened to it and had determined what was on the tape and had written it out for him to type?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. If we ourselves later found that something was not quite right and if he found something, we would rewind the tape and transcribe it again. Because sometimes there would be some kind of distortion. There would be thunder, so some word wouldn't be quite clear. What was important -- then sometimes we would play that back again and take it down again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it when this would be happening, you would have your notebook in front of you so you could follow along what you or your colleagues had written out as the tape was being replayed at the request of the person who had some questions encrypting it or typing it out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: No. The book was in front of him. He was the one who was typing it out, and if something was not clear to him, he would call us, he would ask us about it and say, well, could you rewind it and listen to it again, and so on. So while he was typing it he would find some things that were not quite right, and then he would ask us. Because I was not able to take the book again and look at it, because it would just take too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you had to go back to your machine --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you had to go back to your machine and try to re-listen to the conversation, as opposed to bringing it over to where the typist was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said. When the operator, the encryption operator started to type the text out, he would type until he came up to something that was unclear. If something like that happened, then he would inform me or the person who took down this telegram to listen to it again. This is unclear, there is a discrepancy here between the information or in the names. Could you please check the information. Then I would sit at the machine, replay the tape, and listen, sometimes with the help of others. And then if I found the mistake, I would tell him, I would say, that's it. And that's the way we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the process --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand the process. Now my next question is: What was the distance between you and the typist? In other words, did you have to take a few steps to get back to the device so you can re-listen to the tape or was it right next to the typist? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can recall now the way the devices were placed, he was sitting at the side so the first device was next to him, and then the next one and the third one and then the fourth one. This is how I recall it. It depends which device received the information. If it was the device right next to him, I would just pass it on to him. If it was at some other device, I would -- I had already handed him over the notebook, so there was no need for me to go up to him. I would just play back the tape and then tell him. That was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Now, we don't have the tapes here; they're no longer available, as I understand it. So we don't have the raw material for us to listen back. Is that your understanding as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and this may be sort of one of those chicken or the egg questions, which came first. But it would seem to me that the handwritten version comes before the typed version. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: The version that is written down in the notebook is the first version. Based on which we know that there is also a telegram that needs to be sent out. So we used the notebook so that the person who is sending it out could say, "I have this telegram and I have this telegram," so that he has a record of things that need to be sent out. If it's an important conversation, if it's not an important conversation -- well, we would tell him, there is something that needs to be sent out. As far as the typing and precision is concerned, it was important because we needed to send information that was as correct as possible on to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you as -- when you were working there, did you go back to check to ensure that whatever was typed out was accurate in comparison to what was written out? In other words, that they matched word for word, comma for comma, period for period, what had been taken down by hand and what was then typed out by somebody who had not even heard the tape-recorded conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That person who did the encryption, he was part of the team. He was a member of the team, just as I was. So everything that he wanted to, he could resolve that with us. If he wanted me to go over everything for him, whether it was correct or not, and if I found that perhaps the words were missing, okay, very well, and so on, it's something that I didn't really pay much attention to. What was important to me was the general meaning of the sentence, of the order. That was the most important thing to me. All the other things that were not so important to me were just greetings and different expressions, saying hello to the child or the wife. All these things were something that we didn't really pay that much attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. Now, we looked at what was marked as P245, that one document that we looked at that apparently is in your handwriting. And then you were shown a transcription -- the one that was typed out later on by someone else. Do you recall that document? If we may provide you with it, P245/A -- well, it would be /B would be the handwritten version and then /D would be the typewritten version. And then /A and /C are the respective translations. So if you could look at /B and /D.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, /B is your handwriting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we've already established that on the very last line of this conversation, an expletive, a couple of words, were added to the typed version.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when I look at your version, there seems to be no dilemma as to the sentence itself: "I'll see what I can do." It's pretty clear. No need for interpretation. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as you sit here today and before coming here today, you did not have access to the tape so we could go back and replay it and see whether the expletive was on the tape or was then added by the typist.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We don't have the tape here, and before coming here today you did not listen to the tape to see whether the language that was included by the typist was in fact on the tape itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to this particular document, I'd like you to -- the Prosecutor showed a variety of differences between the handwritten version and the typed version, but I want to point out one particular one. If you can locate where it says "Krle," that line, it's -- I believe it's, you know -- towards the top of the page it says: "Krle, you have to understand. I can't explain it to you." Can you find that line? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, I found the sentence that goes like that, but it's not the same. Yes, I found both the written -- the handwritten and the typewritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in the typewritten version it has a couple of words extra. It says: "I can't explain it to you like this." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, my real interest is for you to go down a couple of lines to where it says in the handwritten version, please. And I'm referring to 245/B, where the gentleman would be looking. And for us it would be 245/A. The line where it says: "I need 15 to 30 men with Boban Indjic. I can't do anything." Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could be so kind as to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could be so kind as to look as the typewritten version that corresponds to that line. Again, it should be two lines down or slightly one sentence after the Krle --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if I can read it to you -- if I can read it back to you it would appear from the translation that we have that the typewritten version says: "I can't do anything without 15 to 30 men with Boban Indjic."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: "I can't do anything without 15 to 30 men with Boban Indjic." Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, it would appear here, sir, would it not, that at least this sentence - and I'm going to use a -- I will say a radical difference, if I could characterise that, between what you wrote down and what is written down. If we just look at it word for word. And maybe radical is too strong. Bold may be a better one, liberal. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Well, I think the meaning of this sentence and the meaning of the other sentence is exactly the same with the exception that here in the handwritten text added at the end you have "There's nothing I can do." At the end. And in the other text it's at the beginning. But I can't see an essential difference as far as the meanings of these two respective sentences are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps you cannot, but then again I did not hear where you were actually an analyst as well as --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. Mr. Karnavas asked the witness a particular question and when he didn't like the answer he's now decided to argue with the witness and that's totally improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that Mr. Karnavas is arguing with the witness. We just want to know, you know, what Mr. Karnavas's interpretation is for those bold differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, are you suggesting that the typewritten version is actually what was on the tape and not the handwritten version that you had put down. If you know. If you don't know, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I know that. I've explained earlier that this is a handwritten text and the other is a typewritten text. And we gave the lad a hand to get it right to type correctly. It's the same meaning. So he probably wrote down what he told him to write, to type. There's really nothing that I can do about this. If I look at this particular case, I don't see any difference there. Perhaps what you want me to say is that these are two different sentences or two different meanings or that the order of the words is not the same. All I can confirm is that the order of the words is not the same. But as for the other two, I don't agree because everything else is identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And my follow-up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My follow-up question to you is: You were not an analyst. You were not trained as an analyst at the time? In other words, to analyse these messages that you were writing down. You were merely to record messages that you deemed important and then faithfully pass them on, right, as they were heard and as they were written out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: We did analyse internally among us. We had to. On our kind of job we had to consult one another. We had to analyse, do some analysis, at least, but the main analysis was carried out by the centre based on our recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall being at your -- working on this particular day, taking this particular message, and writing down this particular message? Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific day. I don't even remember what the weather was like or who was in the room at the moment. I really can't remember. I do know, however, that I recorded this and that I was the one who copied this into the notebook. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you know that because you recognise your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. I know, because at that time I was at Konjuh. I was at the location, but I can't say for sure what the day was or the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I guess what I'm trying to get at, other than -- the only way you know, the only reason you know that this is -- that you wrote this down, that you listened to this conversation and you wrote it down is because you can recognise your own handwriting in that particular notebook. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That's not the only reason. The reason is I know I was there at that time. I spent this period of time right there. I wrote this down. I recognise my handwriting. Even if this document bore a different date, I would perhaps say, "Well, it's not 100 per cent certain I wrote down this date." But this way I really can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I stand corrected. That is the other reason. But my question to you is: As you sit here today, can you tell us whether you did, in fact, have a conversation with the typist who was having a dilemma in trying to figure out what you had written out in this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now, just very briefly, if we could -- if I could take you to those other documents that were shown to you and that you had an opportunity to look at prior to coming here today, and I'm going to refer to again the same documents that you have, which would be /B, 245/B, and the other handwritten transcript, the other handwritten intercept that was from Okresanica, and that would be P245/G. And the respective English versions would be /A and /F. Now, as you've told us before coming here today, you had an opportunity to sit down with the Prosecutor, I assume yesterday or today, to look over these two handwritten intercepts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor asked you specifically to see whether you could compare and contrast to see, one, whether they were basically the same conversation, and two, whether there were any differences. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear that with the exception of the first part, that is, the initial part of the conversation that is not included in your handwritten version for which you have given us an explanation, it would appear that your handwritten version contains more information or different information than the one contained in the other handwritten intercept that was taken down by your colleagues in Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that one contains more information than the other. What I would say is that here I heard both participants, whereas on the other one I can't see the second participant being received. Now, as to more or less information, that's really not something that I have considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you were asked to look at them and to see whether they area verbatim, for instance. Whether one matches word for word with the other. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Word for word, no, not word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They didn't ask you to actually critically look at these two intercepts to see whether there were portions that were missed, either by you or by the other party that were listening in to the same conversation from two different locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes. I may have misunderstood your question. I apologise for that. I thought you were asking me whether it was my opinion that my telegram and his were identical word for word. That's why I said what I said. I did, however, process both these telegrams word for word to check out the discrepancies and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have as well. And correct me if I'm wrong, there are certain passages that are included in your handwritten version that are not included in the other handwritten version. Would you agree with me on that or would you prefer that we go step by step?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I would agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I understand it from your explanation that one reason may be because from your location you were able on that particular day to receive that message -- to tap into that conversation better than your colleagues in Okresanica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean by better. Do you mean more accurately? What do you mean by better? A clearer signal or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A clearer signal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: At Konjuh, the signal, as a rule, was clearer. You must bear in mind the altitude, the difference, that was certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so -- now, I take it even where you were located, there were times when you would pick up a signal, you would begin hearing a conversation, but there were parts that you could not hear or were indiscernible, you couldn't make out exactly what was being said. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Correct. There were many reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, part of the procedure was, at least the way I understand it and the way it has been explained by your colleagues who have come here to testify, that on those occasions the practice would be for the person who is writing out what had been tape recorded to put dots in areas where they were unable to hear what was being said or unable to understand what was being said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Normally there was a word that you couldn't make out, he would put dots there. So there was a part of the sentence that was missing. We used a question mark whenever we weren't quite certain what it was. You would put something in the brackets if there was a piece of information that was ambiguous. This was not a strict rule, but each of us had our own systems and if something was unclear we would just go back to that person for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What if there was a pause, for instance, a fairly lengthy pause, because it would appear if you were able to hear certain portions and they were not able to hear, perhaps there was just a pause, they didn't hear anything, what would you do on those occasions? How would you mark that pause?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: This depends on the situation. I can tell you the following: If we were busy with another piece of equipment and there was a conversation that was underway on the previous piece of equipment, whatever the pause was, the break in the recording, we had to be busy elsewhere and we couldn't operate the first machine. Sometimes it was difficult to go back to the first machine and press the pause button. It was only when we were standing by a particular piece of equipment that we could react quickly enough to press the pause button and react in a timely manner, depending on the situation, but this was not, strictly speaking, a rule that we applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't clear on my question, so I'm going to ask it slightly differently. What if in the conversation you were hearing, in the conversation you were hearing for a second or two seconds you didn't hear anything? In other words, there would be a pause in the conversation, not that you would press the pause button. On those occasions, would you mark down on your notebook, would you make some kind of mark, three dots, something, that would reflect that there was a period of time where there was silence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't use anything, but I can't talk about what the others did. Personally, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that I can finish my cross-examination before the end of this session. Just for the first couple of questions, may we go into private session, because they concern the witness's personal data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it is our intention to send this witness back, because this is the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honour. That's exactly as I intended to do. And I believe I can finish before the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll proceed now, Witness. All the witnesses we had this week, most of them were actually ham radio operators. Am I right in claiming that experienced and qualified people were the ones usually doing this job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: At the outset, yes. But later on, you had all kinds of jobs being done and some people were trying to join, some people were reluctant to join, sometimes some people were free to join and wanted to join. Not all of them were ham radio operators. At the very outset, though, as a rule, the people were amateur radio operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Will you then agree with me that in order to do this job, you needed experience in ham radio operating and you needed to have good ears, a good pair of ears on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I put this differently. Not all the people who were there were radio amateurs, ham radio operators. It would usually take a day or two for them to familiarise themselves with the equipment. The equipment was comparatively simple to use. All you needed was a good pair of ears and then everything else was easy. You needed to be able to hear distinctly. Everything else was simple as far as the equipment was concerned. Anyone could get the grip of it in a day or two. The ham radio operators had to set up the whole thing at the very beginning. They had to be familiar with the frequencies and everything. They had to know exactly where the signals of the Army of Republika Srpska could be captured. So they facilitated the whole process, but only at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you help me with this, please. Can you explain, if you know, what the term operativno maskiranje means in the context of anti-electronic warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: I really can't say. I'm sorry. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you trained in this line of work during anti-electronic warfare? Did they tell you that often misinformation is deliberately spread to deceive the enemy, false trails being laid out concerning places, events, directions of attack, people using false names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: In our line of work, this was not very important. Our work was to listen and to convey. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to ask you. The way I understand your statement, your primary task was to take down those intercepted conversations as accurately as possible, transcribe them, and send them on to your superior command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you never verified information concerning the speakers. Your task was only to transcribe the information as accurately as possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, but on the other hand there was always something important being discussed, you would be there for seven or ten days in a row. If there was something we didn't understand, we needed to discuss things and we often did, what could this be or what could that be. That was an internal matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Whose task was it then to verify the authenticity of information contained in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: That was down to the centre, that they would do that once they processed the information. They had different methods of verifying information, but we were not familiar with that. That's in as for as there were any verifications at all. We just didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To all practical intents and purposes, this means that the verification of authenticity of these intercepts of false information provided by speakers would be faithfully transcribed and forwarded for further processing to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: We did as we saw fit. We were people on the ground and they were back there sitting in their offices. It did very much depend on us. We were the ones who determined the meaning of the sentences. We were the ones trying to make sense of it and to convey the meaning as faithfully as possible. Because if we got something wrong, then inaccurate information was being passed on. The main thing was to get the gist, the general meaning of a given conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I just clarify this. If you heard, for example, that a man named General Vilotic was a speaker, you will try to transcribe this as faithfully as possible, to take it down into the notebook, copy it, and transcribe this. Without going further into probing whether such a person really existed, this General Vilotic, you would not analyse this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will just ask you to make a short pause after my question for the benefit of the interpreters, since we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I had to be told, too, don't worry. Thank you. During your cross-examination today, you said that at Konjuh you had no where, no particular place, to spend your spare time and you were spending all your time in the room where you worked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: No, not all the time. I apologise for this inconsistency. You can't spend all your time in one room. We were only inside if it was too cold to be outside. If we couldn't go out to get some fresh air because it was too cold, the temperature was too low. But since the wind was strong up there, it was a strong, biting wind, the weather was different up there. On account of this, we spent most of our time in the same room where we worked. Some people would watch TV and some people would just toy around with the equipment, even if they weren't on duty. It's an interesting life you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does this also mean that while you were socialising, you sometimes tried to join forces and make some sense out of certain conversations that you had recorded, take it up collectively, in a manner of speaking, raise an issue and try to get to the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-121
utterances.text: We did not try to decipher anything. There were other people who were in charge of that. We were in charge of tapping, listening. We were eavesdropping. What we talked about among ourselves was, for example, about Krle, what he said about his wife as he spoke on the frequency and could he be now, what could his location be.
